![Finished Tennessee tornado map showing stamped hexagons and red string tornado tracks.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/tornado-map-hero.webp)

After watching my former student and Maker Extradoirare Tracy Homer dominate the mapping contest at various TNGIC conferences over the last few years, I knew I'd never be able to match her expertise and creativity in creating physical map objects. So I did the obvious thing and asked if she'd like to work on a project together for the Fall 2026 TNGIC East Fall Forum with me. Combining Tracy's expertise in laser engraving and middle-school memories of making sgtring art, this project combines both concepts to map tornado data for Tennessee as a physical mapping product. As a novice in making physical maps, there were plenty of challenges that I did not initially anticipate, but thankfully Tracy was always there with her no-fear attitude and confidence that we would find a solution. 

The finished map shows the frequency of recorded tornado tracks across Tennessee using stamped hexagons, while the strongest tornadoes, F/EF4 and F/EF5 events, are represented with nails and red string. I am indebted to Tracy for helping me translate what began as a digital cartographic design through an iterative experimentatino process converting GIS geometry, classification, and symbology into wood, ink, metal, and thread.

The project was developed collaboratively by **Michael Campanovo** and **Tracy Homer**, combining GIS/cartographic design with fabrication expertise.

## The cartographic idea

The physical map communicates two aspects of Tennessee tornado history:

1. **Frequency** — where tornado tracks have occurred most often.
2. **Extreme events** — where the strongest F/EF4 and F/EF5 tracks occurred.

The final hexagon classes are:

- **1–5 tornadoes**
- **6–10 tornadoes**
- **11–20 tornadoes**
- **21–30 tornadoes**
- **31–59 tornadoes**

![ArcGIS Pro map design showing the Tennessee hexagon frequency surface and extreme tornado tracks before fabrication. Note that some ideas from the digital version did not make it to the final, physical map. ](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/digital-map-design.webp){fig-cap="The digital cartographic design in ArcGIS Pro before export for fabrication."}

## Designing a GIS map for fabrication

Designing for fabrication changed decisions that would normally be trivial in a digital map. A line on a screen can be arbitrarily short. A physical tornado track represented by two nails and string cannot.

### Generalizing the shortest tracks

Several very short tornado tracks did not provide enough physical distance for two pilot holes, nails, and string. Those tracks were selectively lengthened for fabrication while preserving their general location and orientation. In addition, the starting and ending points of some tornado tracks were moved slightly to avoid overlapping with the labels inside each hexagon. The final map is a compromise between geographic accuracy and physical feasibility.

![Close-up of a short tornado track that required selective lengthening for physical fabrication.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/short-track-generalization.webp){fig-cap="Several very short tracks were selectively generalized so two nails and a string segment could be placed at the final map scale."}

> **Design challenge:** A cartographic symbol that works perfectly on screen may be physically impossible to build at the final map scale.

## Moving from GIS to the laser cutter

ArcGIS Pro remained the geographic and cartographic master. The final geometry was exported as an **SVG** file, preserving vector linework for fabrication.

![Large plywood Tennessee tornado map being engraved in the laser cutter.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/laser-engraving-map.webp){fig-cap="The 18 × 36 inch map during laser engraving."}

![Freshly laser-engraved plywood tornado map before color, nails, and string were added. Note all the burn marks that would require sanding to remove.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/fresh-from-laser.webp){fig-cap="The engraved map before the hand-applied frequency colors and extreme-track string layer were added."}

For those of us growing up in the 1990's, our introduction to the world of tornadoes and storm chasers was through Bill Paxton in Twister. We added a small engraving in his honor to the marginalia of the map. The small flying cow is a nod to the movie's memorable scene where a cow is lifted into the air by a tornado.

![Small engraved flying cow Easter egg included in the map marginalia.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/flying-cow-easter-egg.webp){fig-cap="A small flying-cow Easter egg was engraved into the marginalia."}

## Building the frequency symbology by hand

The hexagon classes were applied manually using archival inks. Tracy fabricated a custom **hexagon-donut stamp** and clear registration jig so each stamp could be centered consistently.

![Using the CO₂ laser to cut out the stamp application guide out of acrylic.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/creating-the-stamping-guide.gif){fig-cap="The custom hexagon-donut stamp and clear registration jig used to align the hand-stamped frequency classes."}

![Tracy used the fiber laser to cut out the custom hexagon donut stamp.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/laser-cutting-the-stamp.webp){fig-cap="Approximately 155 hexagons were stamped individually using archival inks."}

Tracy stamped all **155 hexagons** individually plus the hexagons in the map legend.

## Turning extreme tornado tracks into string

We drilled pilot holes at track endpoints, installed nails, and added red embroidery floss between them. We used two red values with different thicknesses to distinguish **F/EF4** from **F/EF5** tornadoes.

![Pilot holes and small nails marking the endpoints of extreme tornado tracks.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/pilot-holes-and-nails.webp){fig-cap="Pilot holes and 4D nails established the physical endpoints for the F/EF4–5 tornado tracks."}

![Red embroidery floss being stretched between nails to create physical tornado tracks.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/stringing-tracks.gif){fig-cap="Red embroidery floss was stretched between track endpoints to create the physical extreme-tornado layer."}

![Close-up of completed red string tracks showing two shades for F/EF4 and F/EF5 tornadoes. The brighter, thicker red embroidery floss is on the lower left. All the other tracks are thinner, darker embroidery floss.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/extreme-tracks-detail.webp){fig-cap="Two red string values distinguish F/EF4 and F/EF5 tornadoes."}

## When the legend needed a second pass

The first engraved legend revealed two late-stage problems - the class-break numbers were visibly misaligned and they were too wide to work with the custom hexagon donut stamp Tracy created. Rather than re-engraving the entire map, we created a revised legend showing just the upper class limits. The revised legend was engraved and cut from **1/4-inch plywood**, finished, stamped, and glued over the original.

![Original engraved legend showing misaligned class-break numbers.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/original-legend-problem.webp){fig-cap="The original legend revealed a late-stage alignment problem with the class-break labels."}

![Replacement plywood legend being engraved, finished, or stamped before installation.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/replacement-legend-fabrication.webp){fig-cap="A revised legend was fabricated separately on 1/4-inch plywood rather than re-engraving the entire map."}

![Completed replacement legend installed over the original engraved legend.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/replacement-legend-installed.webp){fig-cap="The finished replacement legend became an intentional raised element of the final map."}

> **Design challenge:** Fabrication errors do not always require restarting a project. Sometimes the best solution is to redesign the problem into a new physical layer.

## Explore the tornado data

The physical map deliberately reduces a complex tornado dataset into tangible symbols. The interactive web map provides access to the underlying geography and additional detail. Give it a minute to load, then pan and zoom to explore the tornado tracks and frequency surface.

## What the physical map changed

The most important lesson from the project was that **a map stops behaving like a GIS layout once every symbol has to become a physical object**.

The transition from digital cartography to fabrication required decisions about minimum feature size, material behavior, registration, tolerances, repair strategies, and how much geographic detail could survive translation into a tactile object.

![Oblique close-up of the finished tornado map showing engraving, stamped hexagons, string tracks, and the raised legend.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/tornado-map-finished-detail.webp){fig-cap="A close-up of the finished map showing the combination of engraving, hand-stamped color, nails, string, and layered legend."}

## Final result

![Finished Tennessee tornado map displayed for viewing.](../../assets/images/projects/tornado-map/tornado-map-final-context.webp){fig-cap="The completed physical map ready for display."}

The completed project combines GIS analysis and cartographic design with laser fabrication, custom tooling, hand-applied color, and string art. The digital companion map preserves access to the underlying tornado data, while the physical version emphasizes the material decisions required to turn geographic information into an object.

## Tools and materials

**GIS and design**

- ArcGIS Pro
- ArcGIS Online / Map Viewer
- SVG vector workflow

**Fabrication**

- 18 × 36 inch plywood map surface
- CO₂ laser cutter/engraver
- Fiber laser cutter/engraver
- Custom hexagon-donut stamp
- Clear registration jig
- Archival inks
- Pilot holes and 4D nails
- Red embroidery floss
- 1/4-inch plywood replacement legend
